# 17. Source Operating Model: Pre-Visit Operating System Full Text



This source operating model is retained because AURA PreVisit is a central product engine. The content is transformed above into application modules, workflows, screens, data models, events, rules, and tests.



The Pre-Visit Operating System

Full Staff Work Before the NP Encounter in a Technologically Advanced, High-Performing Primary Care Clinic

Prepared for Dr. Gabbert | May 2, 2026

Contents

1. Executive summary: what the staff accomplishes before the NP arrives

2. The staff model and role map

3. Master timeline from panel intelligence to NP handoff

4. Workstream detail: every pre-visit function

5. Revenue cycle embedded in pre-visit work

6. Quality, outcomes, and safety embedded in pre-visit work

7. Technology stack and automation architecture

8. Dashboards, KPIs, and control limits

9. Staff checklists and handoff templates

10. Governance, compliance, and continuous improvement

11. References

1. Executive summary: what the staff accomplishes before the NP arrives

In the best version of an NP-run primary care clinic, the NP walks into the room with the patient already financially cleared, clinically prepared, risk-stratified, quality-gap mapped, and emotionally oriented to the visit. The NP should not be discovering basic barriers, lost records, inactive coverage, missing authorizations, incomplete histories, or unaddressed preventive opportunities for the first time during the encounter.

The staff's pre-visit work is the clinic's central operating advantage. It converts primary care from reactive visit handling into a panel-based, data-driven, team-based production system. The aim is not merely a smoother appointment. The aim is higher quality, better outcomes, higher patient trust, more complete documentation, fewer denials, greater NP throughput, less burnout, and more appropriate capture of billable preventive, care-management, transitional-care, behavioral-health, and chronic-care services.

1.1 What 'done before the NP' means

Clinical readiness: the chart is reconciled, records are obtained, recent utilization is known, medications and allergies are updated, care gaps are identified, relevant questionnaires are complete, and protocol-allowed orders or tests are queued.

Revenue readiness: the patient is scheduled to the right visit type, coverage and benefits are verified, network and PCP assignment issues are resolved, referrals and authorizations are complete, patient responsibility is estimated, and services with payer-specific rules are flagged.

Quality readiness: evidence-based preventive and chronic-disease opportunities are visible, measure denominators and exclusions are checked, health equity barriers are documented, and patient outreach has already begun when possible.

Human readiness: the patient knows why they are coming, what to bring, what forms to complete, what costs to expect, how to use the portal or telehealth platform, and who to contact for barriers.

NP readiness: the NP receives a concise, trustworthy pre-visit intelligence packet rather than a chaotic chart.

1.2 The ideal output: the one-page NP handoff

At the moment before the NP sees the patient, the staff produces an integrated handoff that contains:

Confirmed patient identity, preferred name, pronouns when provided, language, interpreter needs, communication preferences, and caregiver or guardian status.

Visit purpose, patient-stated agenda, staff triage concerns, and any time-sensitive abnormal findings.

Coverage, benefit, authorization, referral, and estimated patient-responsibility status.

Eligibility for AWV/IPPE, TCM, CCM, APCM, PCM, RPM/RTM, BHI/CoCM, CHI/PIN, ACP, vaccines, preventive screenings, procedures, labs, and other services, with payer-specific caveats.

Medication list, allergy list, refill needs, adherence concerns, pharmacy, PDMP checks when applicable, drug-interaction flags, and formulary barriers.

Recent admissions, ED visits, specialist visits, imaging, lab results, external records, and pending outside information.

Quality gaps, risk-adjustment evidence, chronic disease monitoring needs, immunization status, and patient-reported outcomes.

Standing orders completed or pended, screenings completed, vitals entered, rooming concerns, and tasks requiring NP decision or attestation.

1.3 Strategic design principles

Front-load everything that does not require NP judgment. The NP's highest-value work is clinical decision-making, relationship, diagnosis, treatment planning, risk discussion, and complex communication.

Turn every appointment into a panel-management event. A single encounter should close as many clinically appropriate gaps as possible.

Build revenue cycle into clinical workflow instead of bolting it on after the visit. Most denials are created before the claim is submitted; the elite clinic prevents them before the encounter.

Use automation as a safety net, not a substitute for accountability. AI and rules engines identify gaps, but named staff own work queues and exceptions.

Never let coding incentives distort care. Staff prepare evidence and payer rules; only the NP's documented assessment and plan support final diagnosis and service reporting.

Primary care quality programs increasingly depend on accurate digital data, reliable value sets, measure-specific exclusions, risk adjustment, patient access, and careful documentation. NCQA's HEDIS MY 2026 technical update, for example, emphasizes frozen technical specifications, updated value set directories, medication lists, and risk adjustment tables for accurate implementation [13]. CMS's Quality Payment Program continues to emphasize MIPS Value Pathways, alignment across programs, and performance thresholds that affect payment adjustment exposure [19].

2. The staff model and role map

The technologically advanced clinic is NP-run but not NP-dependent for every task. It uses a team model in which every staff member works at the top of their licensure, training, and authorization. AAFP's advanced team-based care discussion describes delegation of agenda setting, history gathering, record retrieval, medication review, EHR navigation, order entry, and visit documentation to trained clinical support staff, while the clinician focuses on clinical decision-making [16]. In an NP-run clinic, the same principle applies within NP scope-of-practice, state law, payer rules, and organizational protocols.

2.1 Staffing ratios and team pods

The elite clinic is built in pods. A high-functioning pod around each NP includes an MA or advanced team assistant, shared RN triage/care management, shared referral/auth support, shared financial clearance, and registry/quality support. AAFP notes that advanced team-based care often requires challenging historical staffing ratios and cites 2.0-2.5 FTEs of dedicated clinical support per physician as an optimal team-based-care benchmark [16]. An NP-run clinic may use similar logic, adjusted for volume, panel acuity, payer mix, and state rules.

One MA or advanced team assistant is assigned as the named pre-visit owner for each session.

A centralized clearance team handles registration, eligibility, benefit verification, estimates, and authorizations before the clinical team touches the chart.

A population-health team supplies registries and gap lists so the MA is not manually discovering quality gaps one chart at a time.

A revenue-integrity specialist maintains a payer-rules library and audits the highest-risk visit types: AWV, TCM, preventive plus problem-oriented E/M, procedures, vaccine visits, care management, and telehealth.

A compliance officer validates that staff tasks stay within scope and that billing is supported by documented patient need and service requirements.

2.2 Supervision, scope, and NP payment guardrails

Medicare recognizes nurse practitioners and other advanced practice registered nurses in the PFS structure, with CMS outlining payment and billing details for NP professional services and incident-to auxiliary services [9]. Staff may gather information, follow approved protocols, queue orders, obtain consent, track time, and prepare documentation support, but final diagnosis, medical decision-making, assessment, plan, and any clinically required attestation belong to the NP or other qualified billing provider. When payer-specific rules differ from Medicare, the clinic follows the stricter operational rule unless the compliance team has approved a payer-specific exception.

3. Master timeline from panel intelligence to NP handoff

The clinic treats pre-visit work as a staged assembly line with hard deadlines, named owners, work queues, and auto-escalation. Every scheduled patient receives a readiness score. A patient is not considered ready merely because an appointment exists; the patient is ready only when clinical, financial, and operational prerequisites are complete or explicitly escalated.

3.1 The readiness score

Each appointment is assigned a dynamic readiness score from 0 to 100. The score is visible in the schedule and huddle board. The score is not a vanity metric; it controls staff escalation and the morning huddle agenda.

Clinical data ready: outside records, labs, imaging, discharge summaries, medications, allergies, problem list, and questionnaires.

Revenue cycle ready: eligibility, benefits, PCP assignment, referral, authorization, estimate, Good Faith Estimate if applicable, ABN or payer notice if applicable, and payment method.

Quality ready: care gaps identified, standing orders pended or completed, registry status updated, exclusions documented, and vaccine registry checked.

Patient ready: portal or phone forms complete, transportation/interpreter/caregiver needs solved, visit purpose understood, and home readings/devices available.

NP ready: concise handoff generated, open decisions listed, and documentation prompts prepared.

4. Workstream detail: every pre-visit function

4.1 Panel intelligence and proactive outreach

The highest-performing clinic does not wait for patients to ask for care. A population-health registry continuously scans the panel for patients who are due, overdue, at risk, recently discharged, or likely to generate preventable high-cost events. AHRQ describes practice facilitation as building primary care capacity for continuous quality improvement and meaningful changes designed to improve outcomes [15]. The clinic internalizes that concept: the registry is the daily operating plan.

Risk tiers are refreshed daily using claims, EHR history, recent utilization, chronic conditions, medication burden, lab trends, social-risk signals, no-show history, and prior hospitalization.

Outreach campaigns target AWV eligibility, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes monitoring, depression follow-up, cancer screenings, immunizations, medication adherence, postpartum or post-discharge follow-up, missed specialist recommendations, and high ED use.

Each outreach record includes patient response, barrier, preferred channel, next step, and whether the outreach itself supports a care-management workflow.

High-value scheduling protocols preserve dedicated TCM, complex chronic care, behavioral health, and preventive-care capacity rather than filling all openings with low-complexity visits.

4.2 Scheduling and visit-type optimization

Scheduling is a clinical and revenue-cycle task, not clerical data entry. The scheduler uses a decision tree that classifies the request into the correct visit family, then routes according to acuity, continuity, service eligibility, and payer rules.

Visit families include new patient intake, established follow-up, urgent/same-day, AWV/IPPE, preventive physical, chronic disease follow-up, medication management, TCM, procedure, nurse/MA protocol visit, vaccine, lab-only, behavioral health, care-management enrollment, RPM setup, and telehealth.

The scheduler flags same-day combinations that may be appropriate and separately identifiable, such as AWV plus problem-oriented E/M, while clearly noting that final billing depends on NP work and documentation.

TCM appointment logic books the face-to-face visit within the required 7- or 14-day window based on complexity while ensuring the interactive contact workflow begins within 2 business days of discharge [6].

Preventive visits are scheduled with enough time to complete the HRA, medication and history review, personalized prevention planning, screenings, and patient education described by CMS for AWVs [1].

Telehealth scheduling confirms the patient's location, technology access, identity verification method, emergency backup plan, and payer policy before the visit.

4.3 Registration, patient identity, and demographic integrity

The clinic treats identity and demographics as clinical-safety and payment-safety infrastructure. A wrong DOB, wrong payer, duplicate chart, stale address, or wrong guarantor can become a denied claim, HIPAA violation, missed result, or medication safety issue.

Verify legal name, preferred name, date of birth, address, phone, email, emergency contact, guarantor, guardian, caregiver access, release-of-information permissions, language, interpreter need, disability accommodations, portal access, pharmacy, and preferred communication channel.

Scan or electronically capture government ID and insurance cards when appropriate, but reconcile the data against payer eligibility rather than trusting the card alone.

Run duplicate-chart detection and merge workflows before chart prep. Every quality measure, medication list, and billing claim depends on accurate patient matching.

Capture race, ethnicity, language, sexual orientation/gender identity when the organization collects it, disability accommodation, and social-risk data with respectful scripting and clear explanation of use.

4.4 Eligibility, benefits, and network verification

Eligibility work is repeated at multiple points: scheduling, 72-48 hours before the visit, and at check-in. Real-time eligibility tools are useful but not sufficient; staff must interpret plan rules, payer portals, referral requirements, PCP attribution, and benefit quirks.

Run EDI 270/271 or payer API eligibility and document active coverage, effective dates, plan type, subscriber/guarantor, Medicaid/Medicare status, Medicare Advantage vs traditional Medicare, secondary coverage, COB, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket accumulation, and carve-outs.

Confirm whether the clinic and NP are in network, whether the patient must name the clinic or NP as PCP, whether a referral is required, and whether the planned service is covered in the selected setting.

Identify benefit differences for AWV, preventive service, problem-oriented E/M, telehealth, lab, diagnostic test, vaccination, behavioral health, care management, and remote monitoring.

Create a coverage exception task when the payer response is ambiguous, the patient's plan appears inactive, PCP assignment is wrong, or the plan has a retroactive termination risk.

4.5 Patient financial clearance and financial experience

The best clinic is transparent before the patient arrives. The financial counselor explains what the clinic knows, what the payer may change, what is due now, and what assistance is available. CMS's No Surprises Act guidance page includes Good Faith Estimate resources for uninsured or self-pay individuals [17]. CMS training materials also note that some requirements apply to providers and facilities for uninsured or self-pay individuals who schedule care or request an estimate [17].

Generate patient responsibility estimates using contract rates, benefit data, diagnosis/service assumptions, and known limitations. Do not present estimates as final payer adjudication.

For uninsured or self-pay patients, provide Good Faith Estimates when required and document delivery method, date, covered services, expected charges, and patient questions.

Offer financial-assistance screening, sliding-fee or charity policy pathways where applicable, and payment plans before the visit becomes a conflict at the front desk.

Collect copay and known patient balances ethically at check-in; avoid scripts that pressure patients away from medically needed care.

Flag likely noncovered services and obtain appropriate payer notices when required by policy before service delivery.

4.6 Referrals, prior authorization, and medical necessity

Prior authorization is treated as a care-access function and denial-prevention function. CMS's 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule focuses on improving health information exchange and prior authorization processes through policy and technology; impacted payers have certain January 2026 provisions and primarily January 2027 API requirements [7]. CMS also states that impacted payers must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, excluding QHP issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges in the referenced FAQ context [8].

Determine whether the visit, procedure, diagnostic service, medication, remote-monitoring device, behavioral health service, or referral requires prior authorization or a PCP referral.

Compile payer-required clinical facts, including prior conservative therapy, prior results, functional limitation, guideline criteria, failed medications, and duration of symptoms.

Use prior-authorization APIs or payer portals when available; track submission date, decision deadline, status, approval number, denied reason, expiration date, authorized units, approved site, and appeal window.

Alert the NP only when clinical clarification is needed. Staff should not interrupt the NP for information already present in the chart or payer criteria.

If the authorization is pending or denied, the flow captain decides whether to proceed, reschedule, convert visit type, or obtain patient notice.

4.7 Health information exchange, records, and diagnostic retrieval

The clinic's HIE/records team prevents the common failure in primary care: the patient shows up, but the hospital discharge summary, specialist plan, imaging report, or outside lab is missing. Records acquisition begins the moment the visit is scheduled and again during the chart scrub.

Pull CCD/Continuity of Care documents from the HIE, ADT feeds, hospital portals, outside lab portals, imaging portals, state immunization registry, e-prescribing history, and payer claims when available.

Request external records with patient authorization when needed, including recent ED/hospital documents, specialist notes, operative reports, imaging, pathology, colonoscopy reports, mammograms, vaccination history, and prior primary-care notes.

Summarize clinically relevant data for the NP without dumping unfiltered records into the encounter. The handoff should say what matters and where the source can be found.

Track missing records as open tasks with due dates. If a critical record is unavailable, the NP handoff states the consequence and decision needed.

4.8 Quality-gap identification and preventive-care preparation

Before every visit, the quality engine checks the patient against clinical measures, payer incentive programs, and internal care standards. The CDC immunization schedule page provides current schedules for healthcare providers and links to adult and child/adolescent immunization schedules [14]. NCQA's HEDIS updates emphasize standardized performance measures and technical guidance for accurate measure implementation [13].

Preventive gaps: AWV/IPPE eligibility, colon cancer screening, breast cancer screening, cervical cancer screening, lung cancer screening criteria, immunizations, osteoporosis screening, hepatitis C/HIV screening, tobacco screening, alcohol screening, depression screening, fall risk, cognitive concerns, and advance care planning.

Chronic-disease gaps: A1c, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, eGFR, diabetic retinal exam, BP control, statin therapy, anticoagulation review, COPD/asthma control, heart failure monitoring, CKD staging, obesity management, pain/function goals, and behavioral health follow-up.

Equity and access gaps: language, transportation, food, housing, medication affordability, digital access, caregiver burden, disability accommodations, and low health literacy.

The MA queues standing orders only when approved protocol criteria are met; the NP sees what was completed, what is pending, and what requires NP decision.

4.9 AWV and preventive-service prework

AWV workflow is a major quality and revenue opportunity, but also a compliance risk. CMS states that the AWV includes a health risk assessment and lists required HRA elements such as demographic data, health status self-assessment, and psychosocial risks [1]. CMS compliance guidance reported a 24.5% overpayment rate for AWVs including subsequent PPPS visits in 2024 Medicare FFS supplemental improper payment data, with a projected overpayment amount of $307.5 million [2]. This is why the elite clinic uses a strict AWV checklist instead of relying on memory.

Verify AWV/IPPE eligibility and prior date before scheduling and again before billing.

Send HRA electronically or complete by phone for patients with portal barriers. Confirm accessibility, language, and literacy needs.

Prepare medical/family history, current providers/suppliers, medication list, allergies, depression screening, functional ability, home safety/fall risk, cognitive concerns, preventive screening schedule, immunization needs, and personalized prevention plan elements.

Identify separately identifiable problem-oriented concerns before the visit, but only the NP's work and documentation determine whether an additional E/M service is billed.

Prepare preventive service eligibility, including vaccines and screenings, and check payer-specific rules for same-day services and modifiers.

4.10 TCM prework

TCM is a high-value transition-of-care workflow that begins before the NP face-to-face visit. CMS describes the 30-day TCM period as beginning the day the patient is discharged and continuing for the next 29 days, and TCM components include interactive contact within 2 business days after discharge, medically reasonable and necessary non-face-to-face services, and one face-to-face visit within the applicable 7- or 14-day timeframe [6]. CMS also notes that only one physician or non-physician practitioner may report TCM services and that services are reported once per patient during the TCM period [6].

ADT feed or daily hospital discharge report identifies eligible patients within hours, not days.

RN or qualified clinical staff contacts the patient/caregiver within 2 business days, addresses status and needs beyond scheduling, documents successful or attempted contact, and continues attempts until successful when required.

Records team obtains discharge summary, medication changes, pending tests, consult recommendations, home health orders, DME needs, and follow-up appointments.

MA or RN schedules the face-to-face visit within 7 or 14 calendar days as appropriate and flags urgency for high-risk discharges.

Pharmacy team reconciles discharge medications against the pre-admission list and pharmacy fill history; urgent discrepancies go to the RN or NP before the visit.

Care coordinator arranges home health, transportation, specialist follow-up, community resources, and patient education.

Revenue-integrity work queue prevents duplicate TCM reporting, global-period conflicts, and missing documentation of discharge date, first contact date, face-to-face date, and medical decision complexity.

4.11 Chronic care, APCM, PCM, RPM/RTM, BHI, CHI, and PIN readiness

The advanced clinic has a care-management eligibility engine. CMS's care management page is the central PFS resource for services including advanced primary care management, chronic care management, transitional care management, and behavioral health integration [4]. CMS's CCM booklet states that eligible CCM patients have multiple chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months or until death, placing them at significant risk, and that CCM services are typically non-face-to-face care coordination services with monthly time thresholds [5]. CMS's APCM page states that auxiliary personnel can provide APCM services incident to the billing provider's services under general supervision, subject to requirements [10].

Identify patients potentially eligible for CCM, complex CCM, APCM, PCM, chronic pain management, BHI/CoCM, CHI, PIN, RPM, or RTM based on chronic conditions, utilization, risk, social need, behavioral health need, and payer coverage.

Confirm that initiating-visit requirements, patient consent, care-plan requirements, time tracking, supervision, and duplicate-billing restrictions are met before services begin.

During pre-visit planning, staff prepares care-management consent language, care-plan template, active conditions, patient goals, barriers, and staff tasks for the NP to review.

For RPM/RTM, staff validates device appropriateness, payer coverage, patient ability to use the device, data transmission pathway, alert thresholds, emergency instructions, and consent.

For BHI/CoCM, staff identifies screening results, psychiatric history, medication history, consent needs, registry enrollment, and care-manager availability.

4.12 Risk adjustment and clinical documentation preparation

In value-based and Medicare Advantage environments, diagnosis specificity and complete chronic-condition documentation affect patient risk representation, contract performance, and care planning. CMS maintains model software and ICD-10 mappings for 2026 risk adjustment [18]. The clinic's staff may surface evidence, but does not decide that a condition is active or codeable. The NP must evaluate, assess, treat, monitor, or otherwise clinically address the condition and document the basis.

The risk engine identifies previously documented chronic diagnoses not yet assessed this year, suspected conditions supported by objective evidence, and discrepancies between specialist notes, labs, medication lists, and the current problem list.

A coder or documentation specialist prepares an evidence summary: source note, date, lab/imaging evidence, medication evidence, and why it matters clinically.

The handoff uses cautious language: 'history/evidence to review' rather than 'code this.'

The NP receives specificity prompts for conditions already clinically relevant to the visit, such as complications, severity, acuity, laterality, stage, control status, and treatment status.

Compliance audits monitor for unsupported diagnosis carry-forward, cloned documentation, suspect-only coding, and pressure to capture diagnoses unrelated to patient care.

4.13 Medication reconciliation and pharmacy optimization

Medication work before the NP enters the room is one of the highest-yield safety and quality functions. It also creates revenue opportunities by supporting medication-management visits, care-management services, quality measures, and chronic-disease outcomes.

Pull pharmacy fill history, e-prescribing data, patient-reported medications, outside discharge meds, specialist prescriptions, OTCs, supplements, and allergies.

Flag duplicates, high-risk medications, renal-dose concerns, anticoagulants, insulin and hypoglycemia risk, controlled-substance issues, missing statin/ACE/ARB indications where relevant, and formulary or prior-auth barriers.

Reconcile medication affordability, adherence, pill burden, pharmacy preference, mail-order use, refill synchronization, and 90-day supply opportunities.

Check PDMP when clinic policy or state law requires it before controlled-substance conversations.

Prepare refill requests and medication questions for NP decision; staff does not independently change therapy outside protocol.

4.14 Patient-reported data and digital intake

The patient should not spend half the encounter answering questions that could have been captured before arrival. Digital intake is adaptive: it changes based on age, sex assigned at birth where clinically relevant, chronic conditions, medications, payer, visit type, and prior answers.

Forms include reason for visit, patient agenda, symptom questionnaires, HRA, PHQ-2/9, GAD-7, AUDIT-C, DAST, pain/function scales, falls, ADLs/IADLs, cognitive concerns, tobacco, social needs, medication list, allergies, home BP/glucose readings, device data, family history, surgical history, and preventive screening history.

The system sends forms by portal, SMS link, email, phone call, or mailed packet depending on patient preference and digital access.

Positive screens generate workflows: suicide-risk escalation, substance-use brief intervention, food insecurity support, transportation assistance, fall-risk review, or urgent symptom triage.

Incomplete forms trigger a same-day plan: front-desk completion, MA completion, interpreter support, or deferral with reason.

4.15 Standing orders, labs, vaccines, and diagnostic readiness

Standing orders are a major differentiator when properly governed. They convert evidence-based care into reliable action while preserving NP judgment for exceptions and decisions outside protocol.

Protocol committees approve standing orders for vaccines, routine chronic-disease labs, urine microalbumin, point-of-care tests, pregnancy tests, EKG routing, spirometry readiness, specimen kits, and follow-up intervals.

MA confirms inclusion and exclusion criteria, contraindications, patient consent, payer coverage, and safety requirements before completing any standing-order action.

Lab orders are checked for medical necessity, recent duplicates, appropriate diagnosis support, fasting requirement, specimen logistics, and payer lab network restrictions.

Vaccination work includes registry check, contraindication screening, VIS delivery where applicable, inventory check, lot/expiration readiness, and documentation pathway.

Abnormal pre-visit data or critical values are routed to RN/NP immediately rather than waiting for the appointment.

4.16 Behavioral health, social need, and safety workflows

The advanced clinic treats behavioral health and social need as routine primary care data, not side notes. Social-risk and behavioral-health data are captured before the NP visit so the NP can make decisions and the team can act quickly.

Screening tools are selected by visit type and patient risk: depression, anxiety, suicide risk, substance use, intimate partner violence, social needs, caregiver strain, loneliness, pain, and cognition.

Positive screens are not merely stored. They create work queues for behavioral health, social work, CHW, RN triage, or emergency escalation.

Staff scripts explain why questions are being asked, how privacy works, and what resources are available.

The handoff clearly distinguishes urgent safety risks, actionable barriers, and routine follow-up items.

4.17 Day-before chart scrub

The day-before scrub is the high-reliability checkpoint. Every patient scheduled for the next clinic day is reviewed in a standardized order. The output is a chart-readiness label: green, yellow, red, or black.

Green: fully ready; no open issues except routine rooming.

Yellow: minor issue that can be completed during rooming or by support staff without disrupting NP flow.

Red: open issue may affect clinical care, billing, safety, or visit completion; requires action before the visit or huddle decision.

Black: visit should not proceed as scheduled without leadership/NP decision, such as inactive coverage for nonurgent elective service, missing required auth, severe safety concern, or wrong appointment type.

The scrub sequence is: identity, visit type, eligibility, auth/referral, estimate, forms/HRA, outside records, recent utilization, meds/allergies, care gaps, standing orders, labs/imaging, risk/documentation prompts, care-management eligibility, patient barriers, and NP handoff.

4.18 Morning huddle and flow design

The morning huddle is the operating room briefing of primary care. It should be short, data-driven, and focused on exceptions. It is not a staff meeting.

Review schedule shape: complex visits, new patients, TCM, procedures, double-booked slots, late-arrival risk, interpreter needs, rooming bottlenecks, and open staffing gaps.

Discuss each red/yellow patient: unresolved auth, missing data, abnormal pre-visit findings, high-risk medication issue, behavioral-health risk, social barrier, or quality opportunity.

Assign same-day owners: who obtains missing record, who calls payer, who escorts patient to lab, who arranges transportation, who handles interpreter, who does warm handoff.

Protect NP focus by routing non-NP tasks to staff before the first patient arrives.

4.19 Check-in and front-desk readiness

Check-in is the final front-end revenue-cycle gate. It also sets the emotional tone of the visit.

Use two patient identifiers, confirm visit type and patient-stated reason, verify identity and insurance, update demographics, confirm consents, collect copay or known balance, and route financial questions to counselor rather than debating at the desk.

Confirm interpreter, caregiver, portal, forms, privacy preferences, and any immediate mobility, sensory, cognitive, or safety need.

Run same-day eligibility recheck for high-risk payer categories and document any change.

If coverage is inactive or authorization is missing, front desk follows an exception script and escalates to flow captain without humiliating the patient.

4.20 Rooming and advanced intake before NP entry

Rooming is not a mechanical vitals process. It is the last clinical-preparation step before the NP encounter.

Confirm patient agenda and prioritize top concerns; identify urgent symptoms that require RN/NP immediate awareness.

Measure and document vitals accurately; repeat abnormal blood pressure when protocol requires; confirm height/weight/BMI and pain score when relevant.

Reconcile medications, allergies, pharmacy, immunizations, social history, tobacco/alcohol/substance use, home readings, and recent care outside the clinic.

Complete screening tools and standing orders; administer vaccines or point-of-care tests only under approved protocols and consent workflows.

Prepare patient for NP: gowning, equipment, specimens, device readings, paperwork, educational materials, and clarification of what has already been handled by staff.

Notify NP immediately for critical vitals, chest pain, neurologic symptoms, suicidal ideation, severe hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia, pregnancy-related danger signs, or other red flags defined by protocol.

4.21 Telehealth pre-rooming

Telehealth visits receive the same rigor as in-person visits. Staff conducts a virtual rooming process before the NP joins.

Verify identity, patient location, emergency contact/location, consent, technology function, audio/video quality, privacy, interpreter, and whether anyone else is present.

Confirm payer telehealth coverage, modality requirements, visit type, and whether the NP is authorized to treat the patient in the patient's location.

Collect home vitals, device data, photos only when appropriate and secure, medication list, pharmacy, and patient agenda.

Escalate immediately when the patient appears medically unstable, reports high-risk symptoms, or cannot safely complete the visit by telehealth.

5. Revenue cycle embedded in pre-visit work

The clinic's revenue-cycle performance is won before the NP enters the room. The claim should be easy to submit because the schedule, payer, authorization, documentation prompt, and service eligibility were correct from the start. CMS describes the PFS as the primary method of payment for enrolled providers' professional services in private practice, incident-to services, diagnostic tests, and radiology services [12]. The elite clinic treats every PFS-facing event as a pre-visit design problem.

5.1 High-revenue services prepared before NP evaluation

The staff does not decide that a service will be billed; staff makes sure the NP has the information, patient consent, documentation framework, and payer context needed when the service is clinically appropriate.

AWV/IPPE and preventive services: eligibility verification, HRA completion, preventive plan preparation, vaccine and screening eligibility, same-day problem-oriented concern flags, and payer rules [1][2][3].

TCM: discharge feed monitoring, interactive contact, discharge record retrieval, medication reconciliation, face-to-face visit timing, and documentation guardrails [6].

CCM/complex CCM: chronic-condition eligibility, initiating-visit status, patient consent, care-plan creation, time tracking, and duplicate-billing controls [5].

APCM: monthly service eligibility, chronic-condition level, QMB status when relevant, performance-reporting readiness, and auxiliary-personnel workflow [10].

PCM: single high-risk chronic condition support, disease-specific care plan, expected duration, and monthly service readiness [11].

BHI/CoCM: positive behavioral-health screens, registry enrollment, consent, care-manager workflow, psychiatric consultant availability, and monthly tracking [4].

RPM/RTM: device eligibility, consent, payer coverage, setup workflow, data transmission, alert triage, and monthly communication requirements.

CHI/PIN: social need or serious illness navigation needs, initiating visit status, auxiliary personnel qualification, resource plan, and documentation.

Vaccines, injections, procedures, labs, and point-of-care testing: coverage, medical necessity, consent, lot/expiration, supply capture, and documentation.

5.2 Coding and documentation prompts before the visit

Pre-visit prompts are designed to prevent missed legitimate revenue and prevent unsupported billing. They appear in the NP handoff and EHR template but do not force billing.

Prompts are service-specific, not generic. Example: AWV prompt includes HRA, personalized prevention plan, depression screening, functional ability, history, and screening schedule; TCM prompt includes discharge date, first interactive contact date, face-to-face date, MDM complexity, and medication reconciliation.

Prompts distinguish staff-completed tasks from NP-required work. This prevents staff work from being mistaken for NP medical decision-making.

Modifier prompts are payer-specific. Staff may flag potential need for modifier 25 or other payer-specific requirements, but final use depends on separate, identifiable, documented service.

Diagnosis prompts show evidence and specificity needs, not revenue value. The wording is compliance-protective and patient-care focused.

Every high-risk code family has a retrospective audit sample and feedback loop.

5.3 Payer-rules library

A payer-rules library is maintained like a medication formulary. It contains plan-specific rules for visit types, preventive services, auth requirements, referrals, telehealth, lab networks, vaccine coverage, care-management services, modifiers, documentation, and timely filing. It also includes payer-specific patient-estimate assumptions and contract rates where available.

Every denial that could have been prevented before the visit creates a payer-rules update.

Rules have owners, review dates, source links, version history, and staff training notes.

EHR and PM edits are updated when possible so staff are guided inside the workflow rather than forced to remember rules.

High-risk payer changes are summarized at huddles and weekly revenue-cycle meetings.

5.4 Revenue cycle staffing work queues

The clinic uses work queues, not inbox chaos. Each queue has a service-level agreement and escalation trigger.

Eligibility issue queue: inactive coverage, PCP mismatch, payer mismatch, COB issue, Medicaid lock-in, out-of-network issue.

Authorization/referral queue: required auth not submitted, pending beyond deadline, denied, wrong site/provider, expired, insufficient units.

Estimate/GFE queue: estimate not delivered, self-pay GFE due, financial-assistance screening incomplete, payment-plan request.

Quality queue: care gaps due, missing exclusion proof, patient declined, standing-order task incomplete, vaccine registry conflict.

Care-management queue: consent pending, initiating visit needed, care plan incomplete, time threshold risk, duplicate billing risk.

Documentation-risk queue: AWV incomplete, TCM timing issue, high-risk modifier, risk-adjustment evidence unresolved, no signature/attestation risk.

6. Quality, outcomes, and safety embedded in pre-visit work

The highest-quality clinic does not rely on the NP remembering every guideline during a 20-minute visit. The staff and technology surface the right information before the encounter. This improves outcomes because the clinic acts on prevention, transitions, medication safety, social barriers, and chronic disease before harm occurs.

6.1 Quality-gap closure as standard operating procedure

Every patient has a gap list tied to age, sex, medical history, payer quality program, internal guidelines, and patient preference.

Gaps are classified as: ready to close today, needs NP decision, needs outside record, patient previously declined, contraindicated/excluded, or not actually due after record review.

Staff prepare the intervention: kit, order, vaccine, referral, patient education, outside record request, or shared decision-making prompt.

Closed gaps are documented in the structured field required for measure reporting, not only in free text.

Declinations and contraindications are respectfully documented with reason and follow-up plan.

6.2 Outcomes improved before the visit

Hypertension: repeat BP protocol, home BP capture, cuff validation, medication adherence review, and lifestyle support before NP decision.

Diabetes: A1c and kidney monitoring due status, eye exam records, CGM/glucose logs, medication affordability, foot-risk prompts, and nutrition/social barriers.

Transitions: discharge contact, medication reconciliation, pending tests, follow-up appointments, home health, DME, and warning signs addressed before NP visit.

Behavioral health: depression/anxiety/SUD screening, suicide-risk escalation, warm handoff readiness, and BHI/CoCM eligibility.

Medication safety: high-risk medication list, interactions, renal dosing, adherence, duplicate therapy, and refill gaps identified in advance.

Preventive care: immunizations, cancer screening, fall risk, tobacco cessation, and AWV prevention plan prepared.

6.3 Equity and access work

Equity work before the visit includes more than documenting SDOH. It requires action before barriers become no-shows, nonadherence, and delayed care.

Language and interpreter needs are booked before the visit, including telehealth interpreter workflow.

Transportation risk is identified 72-48 hours before, with ride coordination or conversion to telehealth when clinically appropriate.

Medication affordability is addressed through formulary review, copay assistance where allowed, 340B or discount pathways when applicable, and pharmacy coordination.

Digital divide is solved by phone intake, mailed forms, in-clinic kiosk, staff-assisted portal setup, or caregiver access.

Food, housing, safety, and caregiver needs generate CHW/social work tasks, not merely ICD-10 or checkbox documentation.

6.4 Patient experience work

Patients receive a clear pre-visit message: what the visit is for, how long it may take, what to bring, expected cost, forms to complete, and how to ask for help.

The front desk uses warm, nonjudgmental scripts for balance, insurance, consent, and delays.

Patients with complex needs are called in advance so they do not arrive to a surprise barrier.

Rooming staff acknowledge the patient's agenda and make sure it is visible to the NP.

The clinic measures patient friction: forms completion time, portal failures, unanswered calls, estimate disputes, and same-day unresolved barriers.

7. Technology stack and automation architecture

The clinic's technology stack is a pre-visit command center. It integrates EHR, practice management, clearinghouse, payer APIs, HIE, patient engagement, referral management, registry analytics, ambient/AI support, and revenue-cycle dashboards. Automation handles detection and routing; staff handle judgment, empathy, exceptions, and patient communication.

7.1 AI governance in the pre-visit system

AI may summarize records, identify likely care gaps, detect missing forms, flag unsupported documentation, propose pre-visit tasks, and draft patient-friendly instructions.

AI may not independently diagnose, finalize codes, decide medical necessity, deny care, or deliver financial/legal conclusions without human-reviewed workflow.

All AI outputs are labeled as draft support. Staff must verify source data before adding anything to the patient chart or NP handoff.

The clinic monitors AI for hallucinated diagnoses, outdated payer rules, bias in risk scoring, missed urgent symptoms, and over-alerting that creates fatigue.

Every AI tool has a data-use agreement, security review, audit trail, privacy review, and downtime plan.

7.2 Interoperability readiness

The clinic prepares for payer and provider interoperability by building workflows that can use APIs when available but still function when a payer portal or fax remains necessary. CMS's interoperability and prior authorization final rule requires impacted payers to implement certain provisions by January 1, 2026, with API requirements primarily by January 1, 2027 [7]. The clinic's pre-visit infrastructure is therefore API-ready but not API-dependent.

Store payer API endpoints, portal credentials, fax fallbacks, and phone escalation paths in the payer library.

Track prior-auth metrics internally: submission-to-decision time, denial rate, approval after appeal, extended review, and reason codes.

Use standardized data fields so HEDIS, MIPS, payer quality programs, and care-management workflows can be reported without manual chart abstraction where possible.

Maintain a patient-access workflow for sharing records, care plans, and visit summaries promptly.

8. Dashboards, KPIs, and control limits

A high-performing clinic does not manage by anecdote. Every pre-visit process has a metric, owner, target, and escalation threshold. The dashboard should show same-day operating risk and trend-level performance.

8.1 Daily dashboard

Today's schedule readiness by patient, visit type, NP, room, and status color.

Open red/yellow issues by owner: eligibility, authorization, records, forms, labs, medication, quality, safety, estimate, interpreter, transportation.

High-risk patients: recent discharge, high ED utilization, abnormal vitals/labs, suicide-risk flag, pregnancy/postpartum risk, anticoagulation, uncontrolled chronic disease.

Expected same-day services: AWV, vaccines, labs, point-of-care tests, TCM, chronic-care enrollment, BHI warm handoff, procedure, imaging referral.

Flow constraints: staff absences, room shortages, interpreter timing, late-arrival risk, supply/vaccine inventory, lab pickup times.

8.2 Weekly revenue-cycle dashboard

Front-end denial rate by payer, root cause, staff owner, and preventability.

Claims held for documentation or coding problems by service type.

AWV, TCM, CCM/APCM/PCM, RPM/RTM, BHI, vaccine, lab, procedure, and telehealth capture compared with eligibility and clinical appropriateness.

A/R days, net collection, POS collections, underpayment variance, refund risk, and write-off reason codes.

Payer issues requiring contract, credentialing, or operational escalation.

8.3 Monthly quality and outcomes dashboard

Quality measure performance and gap closure by panel, payer, NP, risk tier, and equity stratifiers.

Outcome trends: BP, diabetes, readmissions, ED utilization, depression response/remission where measured, medication adherence, and preventive screening completion.

Patient access and continuity metrics: time to appointment, continuity with chosen NP/care team, after-hours access, and portal response time.

Care-management effectiveness: enrolled patients, active care plans, monthly contact completion, hospitalizations, patient goals, and escalations.

Clinical-safety events and near misses traced back to pre-visit failures.

9. Staff checklists and handoff templates

The following templates define what staff actually do. They can be converted into EHR task lists, checkboxes, and huddle boards.

9.1 Seven-day pre-visit chart scrub checklist

Confirm visit type, agenda, modality, NP assignment, slot length, and patient priority.

Verify identity, demographics, language, interpreter, caregiver/guardian, consent, portal, and preferred contact.

Run eligibility, benefits, PCP assignment, network, referral, authorization, secondary payer, and patient responsibility estimate.

Request missing outside records, discharge summaries, consult notes, labs, imaging, procedures, and immunization registry data.

Run quality-gap report and mark each gap as due today, needs NP decision, already completed outside, not due, excluded, or declined.

Send visit-specific forms: HRA, symptoms, PHQ/GAD, SDOH, medication list, home readings, and any condition-specific tools.

Review medication fill history, allergies, pharmacy, refill needs, high-risk meds, and formulary issues.

Identify potential AWV/IPPE, TCM, CCM/APCM/PCM, RPM/RTM, BHI, CHI/PIN, vaccines, labs, screenings, and procedures.

Prepare risk-adjustment evidence and chronic-condition review list for NP evaluation, using compliance-safe wording.

Assign unresolved tasks to named owners with due dates.

9.2 48-hour financial clearance checklist

Re-run eligibility and document active coverage, plan type, and payer response date/time.

Confirm NP and clinic network status, PCP assignment, referral, and authorization status.

Generate patient responsibility estimate or Good Faith Estimate workflow when required.

Contact patient for coverage discrepancies, self-pay status, inactive plan, or high expected balance.

Offer financial assistance screening and payment plan if appropriate.

Document conversation, delivery method, patient questions, and unresolved issues.

Escalate unresolved coverage/auth problems to flow captain before the huddle.

9.3 TCM pre-visit checklist

ADT/discharge report identifies patient and discharge date.

Clinical staff performs interactive contact within 2 business days and documents contact date, method, status, needs, and follow-up plan [6].

Obtain discharge summary, medication list, pending tests, discharge diagnosis, consult recommendations, DME/home-health orders, and warning signs.

Schedule face-to-face visit within 7 or 14 calendar days as clinically and coding-appropriate [6].

Medication reconciliation completed or prepared on or before the face-to-face visit date [6].

Coordinate home health, specialists, transportation, community services, and patient education.

Check duplicate TCM billing risk; document discharge date, first interactive contact date, face-to-face date, and MDM complexity fields.

9.4 AWV pre-visit checklist

Verify eligibility and prior IPPE/AWV date before scheduling and before billing [2].

Complete HRA before or during AWV; accommodate language, literacy, disability, and digital access needs [1].

Update medical/family history, current providers, medications, allergies, functional status, fall risk, depression screen, cognition concerns, and social risks.

Prepare personalized prevention plan, screening schedule, immunizations, and patient education.

Flag problem-oriented concerns separately; final billing depends on separate identifiable NP evaluation and documentation.

Audit AWV documentation completeness because AWV improper payments have been a CMS compliance concern [2].

9.5 Same-day rooming checklist

Use two identifiers, confirm agenda, and ask: 'What is the one thing you most need the NP to address today?'

Review vitals, pain, fall risk, depression/anxiety/substance-use screens, SDOH screen, home readings, and device data.

Reconcile medications, allergies, pharmacy, recent outside care, immunizations, and refills.

Complete standing orders and specimens per protocol; document consent and contraindication checks.

Escalate critical vitals, severe symptoms, suicidal ideation, concerning pregnancy symptoms, or other red flags immediately.

Give NP a structured handoff with patient agenda, red flags, completed tasks, care gaps, RCM flags, and decisions needed.

9.6 NP handoff template

10. Governance, compliance, and continuous improvement

The advanced clinic's pre-visit operating system is powerful only if governed. Without governance, the same system can become alert fatigue, privacy risk, unsupported coding, patient financial friction, or staff overload.

10.1 Compliance controls

State scope-of-practice and supervision review for every delegated task and standing order.

Credentialing and payer enrollment verification for the NP and all billing practitioners before services are scheduled under their NPI.

Coding and documentation audits for AWV, TCM, chronic care, care management, telehealth, preventive plus problem-oriented visits, procedures, and risk-adjusted diagnoses.

Patient consent audits for CCM/APCM/PCM/RPM/RTM/BHI and other services requiring consent or cost-share disclosure.

HIPAA and minimum-necessary training for records retrieval, HIE use, texting, portal messaging, caregiver access, and AI tools.

Patient financial communication review for estimates, Good Faith Estimates, collections scripts, financial assistance, and notice workflows.

AI tool review for data security, accuracy, bias, audit logs, and human verification.

10.2 Weekly improvement rhythm

Monday: panel outreach priorities and quality gaps.

Tuesday: revenue-cycle denials, auth failures, eligibility issues, and front-end fixes.

Wednesday: care-management enrollment, high-risk patients, TCM performance, and social-need barriers.

Thursday: documentation/coding audit feedback and EHR template improvements.

Friday: patient experience, staff workload, schedule design, and bottleneck review.

10.3 The no-blame failure review

Whenever an NP enters a visit and discovers a preventable missing item, the clinic logs a pre-visit defect. Defects are not used to shame staff; they are used to redesign the system.

Clinical defect: missing record, missing med list, missed abnormal result, missed safety flag, missing questionnaire, missed care gap.

Revenue defect: inactive coverage discovered at check-in, missing authorization, wrong visit type, missing estimate, missed billable service prep, payer rule missed.

Experience defect: patient confused about purpose, cost surprise, repeated forms, portal failure, interpreter missing, transportation barrier unaddressed.

System fix: update protocol, automation rule, queue owner, training, payer library, template, reminder timing, or huddle process.

10.4 What makes the clinic exceptional

Most clinics think of pre-visit work as chart prep. This clinic thinks of it as the operating system for quality, revenue, access, and outcomes. By the time the NP sees the patient, the care team has already done the invisible work that determines whether the encounter will be clinically excellent, financially clean, patient-centered, and measurable.

The patient is ready because barriers were solved before arrival.

The NP is ready because decisions, not chores, remain.

The claim is ready because denial risks were handled before service.

The quality measures are ready because gaps were found and routed before the visit.

The outcomes are better because transitions, medications, social needs, and preventive opportunities were addressed before the disease worsened.

The staff are more effective because every task has an owner, deadline, dashboard, and escalation path.

Appendix A: Convert this document into EHR/PM build

The operating model becomes real only when embedded in the technology. The following build map translates the document into system configuration.

Appendix B: Example patient journey

Patient: 72-year-old established Medicare Advantage patient with diabetes, hypertension, CKD stage 3, depression history, recent ED visit for dizziness, overdue AWV, no A1c in 7 months, no urine albumin this year, uncertain pneumococcal vaccine status, and transportation concerns.

Panel engine identifies AWV due, chronic-disease labs due, medication adherence risk, ED follow-up need, and transportation barrier.

Scheduler books a combined AWV/chronic-disease follow-up slot only after confirming adequate time and payer rules; patient agenda is captured.

Eligibility team confirms MA coverage, PCP assignment, copay, lab network, and no referral requirement for the primary-care visit.

Financial counselor sends estimate; CHW confirms transportation and caregiver attendance.

Records team pulls ED note, EKG, labs, imaging, and discharge instructions.

MA sends HRA, PHQ-9, fall-risk questionnaire, medication form, and home BP/glucose request.

Pharmacy technician pulls fill history and flags missed antihypertensive refill and SGLT2 cost concern.

Quality analyst flags A1c, urine albumin, eGFR, retinal exam, BP control, vaccine registry check, fall-risk screen, depression follow-up, and advance care planning discussion.

Risk specialist notes prior CKD and diabetes with complication evidence for NP review, without instructing coding.

At rooming, MA repeats elevated BP per protocol, documents home readings, reconciles medications, completes fall-risk screen, checks vaccine registry, and pends protocol labs.

NP handoff states: ED dizziness follow-up, elevated repeated BP, med nonadherence/cost concern, AWV tasks complete, labs due/pended, vaccine uncertainty, CKD/diabetes specificity to assess, transportation solved, and patient wants to prioritize dizziness and medication cost.

Scope. This document describes work done by staff before the nurse practitioner sees the patient. It includes the weeks before a scheduled visit, the day-before chart scrub, same-day check-in and rooming, and the final handoff immediately before the NP enters the exam room or launches the telehealth encounter. It is an idealized model for an outpatient U.S. primary care clinic and must be adapted to state scope-of-practice law, payer contracts, credentialing status, and organizational compliance policy.

Revenue principle. The clinic maximizes appropriate, compliant revenue by eliminating preventable denials, matching services to patient need and payer rules, documenting accurately, and ensuring no clinically appropriate service is missed. It does not maximize revenue by upcoding, unnecessary care, duplicate billing, or coercive patient financial practices.

Role | Pre-visit work owned | Why it matters

Access center / scheduling concierge | Converts requests into correctly classified visits; triages access; assigns slot length; confirms modality; captures patient-stated agenda. | Prevents wrong-visit scheduling, lost AWV/TCM opportunities, avoidable no-shows, and visit-type mismatch denials.

Registration and identity specialist | Verifies demographics, identity, guardianship, consent status, language, contact preferences, portal access, and duplicate-chart risk. | Prevents claim rejections, patient matching errors, portal failures, privacy errors, and misdirected bills.

Eligibility and benefits specialist | Runs real-time coverage checks; confirms PCP assignment, network status, COB, copay, deductible, coinsurance, carve-outs, and plan rules. | Reduces eligibility denials, out-of-network leakage, uncollectible balances, and surprise patient responsibility.

Financial counselor | Creates estimates, explains patient responsibility, obtains Good Faith Estimates for self-pay/uninsured when required, offers financial assistance and payment plans. | Improves patient trust, point-of-service collection, charity policy compliance, and bad-debt prevention.

Referral and prior-authorization coordinator | Determines referral/authorization needs; compiles documentation; submits to payer portal/API; tracks decisions, expiration dates, and appeals. | Prevents auth denials, delayed care, duplicate tests, and payer medical-necessity failures.

Pre-visit medical assistant | Performs chart scrub, advanced rooming, vitals, screening tools, medication and allergy updates, standing-order tasks, vaccine registry checks, and care-gap preparation. | Increases NP capacity, closes quality gaps, and improves documentation completeness.

RN care manager / triage nurse | Reviews complex symptoms, discharge transitions, abnormal pre-visit data, high-risk medication issues, TCM outreach, and escalation pathways. | Improves safety, avoids missed acuity, and supports TCM and chronic-care continuity.

Clinical pharmacist or pharmacy technician | Pulls medication fill history, formulary information, prior-auth status, interactions, adherence barriers, refill needs, and pharmacy details. | Improves medication safety, adherence, STAR/HEDIS measures, and prescription-related revenue capture.

Behavioral health care manager | Screens for depression, anxiety, substance use, suicide risk workflows, collaborative care eligibility, and warm handoff needs. | Improves outcomes and captures BHI/CoCM opportunities when criteria and consent are met.

Community health worker / social worker | Screens and acts on transportation, food, housing, safety, caregiver, and health literacy barriers; coordinates community resources. | Improves visit adherence, equity, chronic-disease outcomes, and CHI/PIN readiness.

Population health / quality analyst | Runs registries, care-gap logic, measure denominator/exclusion logic, outreach lists, and performance dashboards. | Turns the visit schedule into a quality and outcomes engine.

Revenue integrity coder / clinical documentation specialist | Maintains payer rules; reviews front-end coding opportunities and documentation prompts; audits visit-type and modifier readiness. | Prevents undercoding, overcoding, missing modifiers, noncovered service errors, and poor risk capture.

Lab/imaging coordinator | Confirms outside results; tracks pending diagnostics; obtains orders; prepares protocol-based labs and imaging; resolves duplicate or medical-necessity conflicts. | Reduces avoidable repeat testing, late results, and diagnostic delay.

IT / automation analyst | Maintains EHR templates, rules engines, RCM workflows, AI chart-scrub tools, dashboards, interfaces, and data quality monitors. | Makes the system scalable and measurable instead of dependent on memory.

Compliance and privacy lead | Monitors HIPAA, consent, scope, supervision, coding, documentation, patient financial communications, and AI governance. | Protects the clinic from avoidable audit, privacy, and billing risk.

Clinic flow captain | Runs huddles, balances schedule risk, reallocates staff, clears bottlenecks, and escalates same-day exceptions. | Preserves throughput, patient experience, and staff sanity.

Timing | Staff work before NP | Revenue/quality/outcome effect

12-4 weeks before / panel cycle | Population-health analyst identifies overdue AWVs, chronic-disease monitoring, immunizations, cancer screenings, TCM candidates from ADT feeds, high ED utilizers, medication nonadherence, high-risk chronic disease, and missed follow-up. Outreach team books visits and resolves barriers. | Creates revenue and quality before demand appears. Converts passive panel into active recall. Supports AWV, chronic care, transitions, preventive services, and value-based performance.

At scheduling | Scheduler classifies visit type, acuity, modality, expected length, patient agenda, PCP/NP continuity, new vs established status, translator need, payer, and payer-specific constraints. | Correct visit type drives correct coding, appropriate time, and correct forms. Prevents under-scheduling complex visits and losing eligible services.

10-7 days before | Registration and eligibility teams verify demographics, insurance, PCP assignment, COB, network, referral requirements, patient responsibility, and consent gaps. HIE and outside-record requests are launched. | Front-end denial prevention begins before the chart scrub. Missing coverage and auth issues can be fixed before the patient arrives.

7-5 days before | Quality analyst and MA generate pre-visit planning packet: care gaps, labs due, immunization needs, chronic-disease measures, prior labs, missing specialty notes, HCC evidence, and questionnaire needs. | Transforms encounter into a care-gap closure event. Ensures quality, risk, and outcomes data are visible at the point of care.

5-3 days before | Referral/auth team submits prior authorizations and referral requests; pharmacy team reviews medication fill history and formulary; MA sends questionnaires and visit prep messages. | Reduces same-day cancellations, delayed diagnostics, medication confusion, and denied services.

72-48 hours before | Financial counselor sends estimates or Good Faith Estimates when required; eligibility is rechecked; no-show risk engine triggers reminders; CHW/social worker contacts high-barrier patients. | Improves patient trust, collections, completion of visit prep, transportation, and attendance.

24 hours before | MA performs final chart scrub; RN reviews high-acuity red flags; coder/revenue integrity checks high-risk visit types; lab/imaging coordinator confirms pending data. | Prevents NP surprise work. Ensures potential billable services are either prepared or consciously deferred.

Morning huddle | Flow captain, MA, RN, NP, and support staff review each patient: readiness score, safety flags, expected services, care gaps, authorizations, rooming tasks, and schedule bottlenecks. | Protects throughput and safety. Staff enter the day with a plan rather than reacting patient by patient.

Check-in | Identity, consent, coverage, patient responsibility, forms, interpreter, portal status, and visit purpose are confirmed. Exceptions are routed to clearance or flow captain. | Prevents wrong-patient, wrong-payer, missing-consent, and uncollectible-service problems.

Rooming / telehealth intake | MA confirms agenda, vitals, medication list, allergies, screenings, device data, immunizations, standing orders, and protocol tasks. Abnormal findings are escalated before NP entry. | Creates the final clinical data set and avoids spending NP time on basic intake.

Immediate NP handoff | MA gives concise structured handoff: patient agenda, readiness gaps, vitals, red flags, quality opportunities, RCM flags, meds, records, and what needs NP decision. | The NP starts at the point of decision, not at the point of discovery.

RCM area | Pre-visit failure prevented | Elite clinic control

Patient access / scheduling | Wrong visit type, wrong provider, insufficient time, unrecognized TCM/AWV/care-management opportunity, wrong location/modality. | Structured visit-type decision tree, schedule templates, TCM discharge feed, AWV eligibility checks, telehealth rules, continuity assignment.

Registration | Claim rejection, privacy error, duplicate chart, guarantor mismatch, wrong payer order. | Identity validation, duplicate-chart detection, insurance-card capture, demographic reconciliation, COB checks, guardianship and ROI workflows.

Eligibility and benefits | Eligibility denial, out-of-network denial, uncollectible patient balance, wrong PCP assignment. | Real-time eligibility at booking, 48 hours before, and check-in; payer portal verification; PCP assignment fix; secondary payer validation.

Authorization/referral | No authorization, wrong authorized site/provider/service, expired authorization, insufficient clinical documentation. | Rules engine, payer portal/API submission, auth work queue, deadline tracking, approval-number capture, denial appeal workflow.

Medical necessity | Noncovered service, missing diagnosis support, payer policy mismatch, duplicate testing. | LCD/NCD/payer policy checks, diagnosis-to-test logic, duplicate-result search, ABN/payer notice workflow when applicable.

Documentation readiness | Undercoding, unsupported coding, incomplete AWV, missed preventive plan, missing TCM contact date, missing chronic-care consent. | Documentation prompts, visit-specific checklists, coder work queues, consent templates, care-plan fields, and post-visit audit loops.

Patient responsibility | Bad debt, patient dissatisfaction, delayed payment, dispute escalation. | Pre-visit estimates, Good Faith Estimates for self-pay/uninsured when required, financial assistance, payment plans, card-on-file policy, clear scripts.

Charge capture | Missed vaccines, procedures, screenings, care-management services, device setup, supplies, or separately identifiable services. | EHR charge router, protocol checklists, vaccine inventory integration, service eligibility flags, staff task completion prompts.

Risk adjustment and value-based revenue | Incomplete chronic-condition representation, unsupported diagnosis capture, poor contract performance. | Evidence summaries, annual condition recapture lists, NP-specific documentation prompts, compliance audit of diagnosis support.

Denials learning loop | Repeated front-end errors and payer-specific misses. | Denial reason dashboard, root-cause owner, payer-rules update, staff retraining, EHR edit update, and weekly prevention huddle.

Technology layer | What it does before NP | Control value

EHR and practice management | Scheduling templates, registration, visit documentation, orders, results, charge capture, care plans, task queues, patient portal. | Single source of truth; discrete data fields for quality and billing; audit trails.

Clearinghouse and eligibility engine | 270/271 eligibility, claim edits, payer connectivity, COB, rejection prevention, real-time benefits when available. | Front-end denial prevention and payer-specific rule surfacing.

RCM command center | Work queues for clearance, auth, estimates, denials, charge capture, coding review, and A/R early warning. | Makes revenue-cycle issues visible before claim submission.

Payer rules and contract library | Plan-specific auth, referral, preventive, modifier, telehealth, lab, and estimate rules. | Prevents staff from relying on memory or outdated payer PDFs.

HIE/ADT interface | Hospital discharge alerts, ED utilization, outside labs, CCDs, specialist data, imaging links. | Enables TCM, medication reconciliation, and safe transitions.

Population health registry | Care gaps, risk tiers, quality measures, chronic disease lists, outreach campaigns, HEDIS/MIPS/value-based contracts. | Turns the panel into a proactive operating list.

Patient engagement platform | SMS/email/portal reminders, forms, HRA, estimates, digital consent, education, two-way texting, no-show mitigation. | Improves completion, attendance, and patient readiness.

Referral and prior-auth platform | Requirement lookup, document collection, payer portal/API submission, status tracking, denial/appeal routing. | Reduces authorization-related denials and delayed care.

Medication intelligence | eRx, fill history, formulary, benefit check, prior-auth, PDMP, interaction and adherence signals. | Supports safety, quality measures, and medication affordability.

Remote monitoring platform | Device logistics, readings, alerts, monthly communication, time tracking, escalation protocols. | Supports chronic outcomes and RPM/RTM compliance.

AI chart-scrub assistant | Summarizes outside records, identifies missing data, suggests quality gaps, detects potential coding/documentation risks, creates draft handoff. | Speeds preparation but requires human verification and audit.

BI dashboard | Access, flow, quality, outcomes, RCM KPIs, staff workload, payer issues, patient experience, and no-show risk. | Turns operations into measurable improvement.

Domain | Metrics | Control target

Pre-visit readiness | Percent of visits green by 24 hours; percent red at huddle; unresolved records; incomplete forms; missing labs; missing meds. | Green readiness >= 90%; red unresolved before first patient < 3%.

Access and scheduling | Third next available appointment; TCM scheduled within 7/14-day windows; AWV recall completion; same-day conversion; no-show rate. | TCM contact and visit timing tracked daily; no-show reduction by risk tier.

Eligibility and registration | Eligibility pass rate; PCP mismatch rate; demographic error rate; duplicate chart rate; check-in rework. | Eligibility verified before visit for 98%+ of scheduled appointments.

Authorization/referral | Auth required identified; auth submitted on time; auth denial rate; pending at visit; overturned on appeal; delayed-care days. | Zero preventable no-auth denials; pending auths visible 24 hours before.

Patient financial clearance | Estimate delivered; GFE delivered when required; POS collection; financial-assistance screening; estimate dispute rate. | No self-pay/uninsured patient arrives without a documented estimate workflow unless same-day urgent exception.

Charge capture and coding readiness | Missed charge rate; AWV checklist completion; TCM documentation completion; care-management consent completion; coding audit pass rate. | 100% high-risk visits pass pre-bill checklist before claim submission.

Denial prevention | Clean claim rate; first-pass acceptance; front-end denial rate; medical-necessity denial rate; auth denial rate; timely filing risk. | Denials categorized by preventability and owner within 5 business days.

Quality care gaps | Gaps closed per visit; vaccine completion; screening orders; chronic-disease monitoring; structured exclusion/declination capture. | Every scheduled visit has a documented gap review before NP entry.

Outcomes | BP control, diabetes control, readmission rate, ED follow-up, medication reconciliation after discharge, depression follow-up, adherence metrics. | Tracked by panel, NP, payer, risk tier, race/ethnicity/language when appropriate.

Patient experience | Pre-visit forms completion, call answer time, portal response time, estimate satisfaction, rooming delays, complaints. | Patient friction items reviewed weekly and tied to process fixes.

Staff reliability | Queue aging, handoff accuracy, huddle punctuality, task completion, error rate, overtime, burnout indicators. | No queue without named owner; aging thresholds visible.

Handoff section | Content

Patient context | Name/preferred name, age, pronouns if documented, language/interpreter, caregiver/guardian, visit type, chief concern, patient-stated agenda.

Safety flags | Abnormal vitals, urgent symptoms, positive suicide screen, high-risk medication, pregnancy/postpartum concern, recent discharge risk, infection control issue.

Revenue-cycle flags | Eligibility/auth/referral status, estimate/GFE status, AWV/TCM/care-management eligibility, payer-specific caveat, notice/ABN need, telehealth compliance issue.

Clinical data | Recent ED/hospital/specialist events, pending results, outside records, labs/imaging, medication changes, pharmacy issues, adherence concerns.

Quality and outcomes | Care gaps due today, chronic-disease monitoring, vaccines, screenings, HEDIS/MIPS/payer measures, exclusions/declines.

Risk adjustment | Evidence to review for chronic conditions, annual recapture needs, diagnosis specificity prompts, and source dates.

Tasks already completed | Forms, HRA, screenings, vitals, standing orders, vaccine registry, labs, specimens, education, referrals, social work, care-management consent.

NP decisions needed | Diagnosis/treatment decisions, order approvals, documentation attestations, complex counseling, separate services, care-plan approval, referrals, escalation.

Build area | Configuration needed

Scheduling | Visit-type decision tree, slot templates, AWV/TCM flags, telehealth modality checks, interpreter fields, patient-stated agenda.

Registration | Duplicate-chart alerts, required demographics, insurance-card capture, guarantor logic, consent status, communication preferences.

Eligibility/benefits | Automated eligibility runs, exception queue, PCP assignment field, secondary payer, patient responsibility estimate feed.

Authorization | Payer rules, auth required flag, approval number, expiration date, units, approved site/provider, appeal status.

Clinical intake | Adaptive forms, HRA, screenings, social needs, home readings, medication updates, allergy updates, device data.

Quality | Measure logic, care-gap list, structured exclusion/declination fields, vaccine registry integration, outreach lists.

Care management | Consent, initiating visit, care plan, time logs, monthly status, duplicate billing alerts, patient goals.

Risk/documentation | Evidence summary fields, diagnosis specificity prompts, annual review lists, compliance notes, audit sample queue.

Rooming | Advanced rooming template, standing-order buttons, abnormal-vital alerts, handoff generator.

Dashboards | Readiness score, queue aging, denial prevention, gap closure, patient experience, staff workload, outcome trends.
